inner_thoughts: I spent LKR 8,000 on photocopying last month. For notes that half my students lost within a week.
The printing shop raised prices again. I'm printing less now, and my students are getting less.
I know I should switch to WhatsApp PDFs but I have a few students without smartphones. I don't know where that leaves me.
nodes.intro_body: Printing is the most visible cost in a tuition teacher's budget — and the easiest to reduce significantly without changing how you teach.

strategies.title: Switch to WhatsApp PDF distribution — not gradually
content_paragraphs: Create a WhatsApp group for each batch. Every Sunday, send the week's materials as a single PDF. Students open the PDF on their phone during class, or screenshot the pages they need.
Most O/L and A/L students have smartphones. For the 1–2 students in a batch who don't, print only their copies. The rest is digital.
That's a 90% reduction in printing overnight — without removing any content.

strategies.title: MCQ practice tests: less printing and less marking
content_paragraphs: A 20-question MCQ practice test can be peer-corrected in class by exchanging papers and reading answers aloud. No collection, no marking pile to take home. 5 minutes.
Design your regular practice tests in MCQ format where the subject allows. O/L and A/L exam papers already include MCQ sections — your practice tests should match.
You're not compromising quality. You're reducing printing and marking simultaneously while aligning to actual exam format.

strategies.title: Negotiate bulk printing prices — most teachers don't bother
content_paragraphs: If you're spending LKR 5,000–8,000/month at the same printing shop, ask for a bulk rate. Shops that handle regular high-volume customers will negotiate.
Alternatively, find the cheapest per-page rate in your area — not just the most convenient shop. Two minutes of research could save LKR 1,500–2,000 per month.
The shop nearest your hall is probably not the cheapest. It's just the easiest habit.

strategies.title: Print only what students actually use
content_paragraphs: Track which materials your students reference versus which ones end up in the bottom of a bag after class. In most classes: the model paper gets used, the notes get lost, the summary sheet stays at home.
Print model papers. Send notes digitally. Stop printing things students lose.
Targeted printing costs 30–40% of blanket printing — for materials that actually reach students.

strategies.title: Create a reusable past paper pack — print once, reuse for years
content_paragraphs: The O/L mathematics syllabus doesn't change annually. Compile a comprehensive 5-year past paper booklet once. Print 30 copies. Collect them at the end of each term.
A reusable pack printed at the start of a 2-year O/L preparation run has a per-student, per-year cost that's a fraction of printing new materials monthly.
The student treats it differently too — a bound booklet with their name on it gets kept. A loose sheet gets lost.

next.label: Hall rent is too high for what I earn

nodes.pain_point: Hall rent is too high for what I earn
inner_thoughts: I pay LKR 30,000 rent for a hall I use maybe 15 hours a week. The rest of the time it just sits there.
After rent and printing, I barely feel like I'm earning what my time is worth.
A teacher I know splits a hall with someone who teaches a different subject. I keep thinking I should do something like that.
nodes.intro_body: Hall rent is the most visible cost — but it's usually not the actual problem. Before moving or downsizing, check whether you're using what you're paying for.

strategies.title: Do the revenue-per-seat analysis before changing anything
content_paragraphs: Hall rent is visible. Half-filled seats are silent. If you're paying LKR 30,000 for a 50-seat hall but running only 25 students, your rent problem is actually an occupancy problem.
Fill the hall before moving to a smaller one. Each additional student makes the same rent cheaper per head.

The math: 25 students at LKR 3,000 = LKR 75,000. Hall rent LKR 30,000. Net LKR 45,000. 40 students: LKR 120,000 revenue, same LKR 30,000 rent. Net LKR 90,000. The hall didn't change — the occupancy did.

cards.desc: Same rent. Net: LKR 90k. Same hall.

strategies.title: Stop renting empty hours
content_paragraphs: If you're renting a hall 6 days a week but only teaching 4, you're paying for 2 days of nothing.
Most hall rental agreements can be renegotiated — or you can switch to a 4-day arrangement. The worst they say is no. Most landlords prefer a reliable 4-day tenant to an empty hall.
Alternatively, rent the hall by the session rather than monthly. More expensive per session, cheaper if you're using fewer than 4 days a week.

strategies.title: Share a hall with a different-subject teacher
content_paragraphs: A mathematics teacher and a chemistry teacher who both teach A/L students don't compete — they complement each other. Their students are the same parents, different subjects.
Split the monthly rent. LKR 30,000 becomes LKR 15,000. That's LKR 15,000 permanently removed from your cost base, with zero change to how you teach.
Find one compatible teacher in your area with a compatible schedule. One conversation, one arrangement.

strategies.title: Know when a hall makes sense (and when it doesn't)
content_paragraphs: A home-based teacher with a waiting list of 10+ students and a current batch of 25+ is ready for a hall. A home-based teacher with 15 students and no waiting list is not.
At LKR 3,000/student, you need 10 new students to cover a LKR 30,000/month hall. If you can't generate 10 new students in the first month of having the hall, you're subsidizing the landlord.
Do the calculation for your own numbers before signing any agreement.

strategies.title: A hybrid model permanently reduces your physical space needs
content_paragraphs: 10 students attending physically + 20 students attending online = the same teaching effort and similar revenue, but a smaller required venue.
A smaller room (cheaper rent) serves the physical students. Online students pay slightly less but have no venue cost for you.
The hybrid model may be the most effective long-term tool for managing venue costs — as online adoption continues to grow.

strategies.title: Calculate your break-even enrollment before committing
content_paragraphs: Before signing any hall agreement: monthly rent ÷ monthly fee per student = number of students needed just to cover rent. That's your break-even number.
Can you realistically recruit that many new students in the first month? If yes, the hall makes sense. If not, the hall eats into your existing income.
One hour of calculation prevents 6 months of regret.

next.label: I'm not sure where my money actually goes

nodes.pain_point: I'm not sure where my money actually goes
inner_thoughts: January was good. April feels empty. I don't know what changed — I'm teaching the same students.
I know money is coming in but I never seem to have any. Something is going wrong somewhere.
Someone asked me what my profit margin is. I had no answer. I don't even know what that means for my class.
nodes.intro_body: Independent tuition teachers should have some of the highest profit margins of any profession. Most don't know their number — and that's the only reason they don't.

strategies.title: Track every expense for one month — just one
content_paragraphs: Hall rent, printing, phone data, transport, stationery. Write down everything you spend related to your tuition business for exactly one month.
Most teachers who do this find 2–3 expenses they'd forgotten existed and 1–2 that are significantly higher than they thought.
The month of tracking isn't about being perfect. It's about seeing reality.

strategies.title: Categorize your costs — four buckets is enough
content_paragraphs: Venue (rent, utilities). Materials (printing, stationery, data). Transport (travel to halls, petrol). Admin (phone costs, any software).
Once you can name the four categories, you can see which one is the problem. Usually it's venue or materials — and both are reducible.
Most teachers who do this exercise find their costs are concentrated in one or two categories, not spread evenly.

strategies.title: Find your hidden waste: cash float losses and venue downtime
content_paragraphs: Cash you collected and can't account for. Hours you paid hall rent for and didn't teach.
In a cash-only system, small discrepancies accumulate. A student you forgot to chase for 3 months is LKR 9,000 gone. A hall rented on a day you cancelled class is LKR 1,000 wasted.
Tracking makes these visible. What's visible can be fixed.

strategies.title: Calculate your actual profit margin — most teachers have never done it
content_paragraphs: Monthly students × monthly fee = gross revenue. Subtract all expenses. What's left is your net income.
At 85%+ margins, independent tuition is an extremely profitable profession — if you track it.
The teachers who grow fastest aren't the ones with the most students. They're the ones who know their numbers.

cards.desc: Typical profit margin for independent tuition teachers
Net from 150 students at LKR 3,000 (5 classes/wk)

strategies.title: Tax preparation is your forcing function for financial clarity
content_paragraphs: The annual income tax filing deadline is November 30. Declaring tuition income requires you to gather all income records and list deductible expenses. Even if you're below the LKR 1.2 million personal relief threshold, this process forces you to know your numbers.
Teachers who do their taxes know their numbers. Teachers who don't, don't.
Regulation is tightening. The teachers who already track their finances will barely notice when licensing and formal requirements arrive.
